user.name: NASA - National Aeronautics and Space Administration

text:
Let's see… a five-letter word for happiness: space! 🦀
 
NASA's Hubble Space Telescope captures the intricate structure of the Krab, er, Crab Nebula in this image.

media.ocrText: A colorful nebula in space with a white haze throughout that is more concentrated in the center with a rippling effect. Gas filaments appear to splash outward from the nebula center, colored yellow, magenta, and blue. A faint black border with right angles at the corners of the images show where the telescope’s field of view stops. Small white stars dot the background. Credit: NASA, ESA, STScI, William Blair (JHU); Image Processing: Joseph DePasquale (STScI)

user.name: NASA - National Aeronautics and Space Administration

text:
This September, we're sending a new crew to the International Space Station!

NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Joshua Kutryk, and Roscosmos cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov will lift off for low Earth orbit as part of NASA's SpaceX Crew-13 mission. During their long-duration mission aboard the station, they'll run experiments to help us learn how to live in space while making life better back on Earth: https://go.nasa.gov/4cs7t6y

media.ocrText: A collage featuring the four members of NASA’s SpaceX Crew-13 mission: from left to right, NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Joshua Kutryk, and Roscosmos cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov. Credit: NASA

user.name: NASA - National Aeronautics and Space Administration

text:
Jordan is the 63rd country to sign the NASA Artemis Accords! 🇯🇴

Countries that join our Artemis Accords commit to a set of principles for peaceful, transparent, and responsible space exploration. These partnerships will enable us to build the future of space together. https://go.nasa.gov/3QovgvC

media.ocrText: This graphic shows the list of countries that have signed the Artemis Accords. Flags from 63 different nations are listed over an image of the shadowed lunar surface. The bottom of the image reads: "United for Peaceful Exploration of Deep Space." Credit: NASA

user.name: NASA - National Aeronautics and Space Administration

text:
Our Curiosity Mars rover has been studying the Red Planet since it first touched down on Gale Crater back in 2012.

Now, a new analysis has revealed the most diverse collection of organic molecules ever found on Mars—informing our search for ancient life: https://www.nasa.gov/missions/mars-science-laboratory/curiosity-rover/nasas-curiosity-finds-organic-molecules-never-seen-before-on-mars/

media.ocrText: A "selfie" of NASA's Curiosity Mars rover, standing against a dark brown Martian landscape. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS

user.name: NASA - National Aeronautics and Space Administration

text:
Making moves toward Artemis III.

With Artemis II safely back on Earth, NASA has begun shipping the core stage for the Artemis III rocket from NASA Michoud Assembly Facility in New Orleans to NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida. 

Artemis III will test rendezvous and docking capabilities needed to land Artemis IV astronauts on the Moon in 2028. https://go.nasa.gov/3QBPsdn

media.ocrText: NASA moved the core stage, or the largest section, of the SLS (Space Launch System) rocket that will launch the crewed Artemis III mission in 2027 from the agency’s Michoud Assembly Facility to the agency’s Pegasus barge in New Orleans on April 20, 2026. The core stage is a 212-feet long orange cylinder oriented on its side. The core stage is resting on stands in front of a large warehouse with a NASA logo on it. Credit: NASA/Michael DeMocker

user.name: NASA - National Aeronautics and Space Administration

text:
Welcome to the NASA Artemis Accords, Latvia! 🇱🇻

Latvia is the 62nd country to sign the Artemis Accords—an international commitment aimed at enhancing the safety, transparency, and coordination of exploration on the Moon, Mars, and beyond: https://go.nasa.gov/4cwris1

media.ocrText: This graphic shows the list of countries that have signed the Artemis Accords. Flags from 62 different nations are listed over an image of the shadowed lunar surface. The bottom of the image reads: "United for Peaceful Exploration of Deep Space." Credit: NASA

user.name: NASA - National Aeronautics and Space Administration

text:
One week has passed since Artemis II returned to Earth after a historic mission around the Moon. We laughed, we cried, and we pushed the boundaries of what’s possible, setting the stage for future innovation and exploration.

We’re just getting started.

text:
We're going back to the Moon. We're going to Mars.

You can be part of the effort by joining NASA Force. Applications open at 1 p.m. EDT: https://www.nasa.gov/careers/nasaforce/

media.ocrText: People sit at desks in a dark room lit by computer monitors and dim overhead lights shaped like hexagons. One person in the foreground points at a screen. Credit: NASA

user.name: NASA - National Aeronautics and Space Administration

text:
LIVE: Want to hear more from the Artemis II astronauts?
 
Fresh off their return to Earth, the crew are holding a news conference to discuss their mission. Tune in now: https://www.youtube.com/live/_43Ei9eQVww

media.ocrText: The astronauts of Artemis II (from left: Jeremy Hansen, Christina Koch, Victor Glover, and Reid Wiseman) stand on stage after a crew return event. They are wearing blue space suits and brimmed caps with their names on them. Wiseman is holding Rise, the mascot and zero gravity indicator of the Artemis II mission. Credit: NASA/Helen Arase Vargas

user.name: NASA - National Aeronautics and Space Administration

text:
Astronauts: They're just like us.
 
While voyaging around the Moon on their historic mission, the NASA Artemis II crew used tablets and smartphones to complete work.

media.ocrText: NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman and Christina Koch smile downward at the camera, while CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Jeremy Hansen, at right, uses a cell phone. Credit: NASA
NASA astronaut Reid Wiseman taps on the screen of a tablet. He is wearing a black hoodie with an American flag patch on its left arm. Credit: NASA
NASA astronaut Reid Wiseman looks upward while holding a tablet. Another astronaut is on the left, but all that's visible of them is their lower body. Credit: NASA

user.name: NASA - National Aeronautics and Space Administration

text:
"The gratitude of seeing what we saw, doing what we did… it’s too big to just be in one body."

In the newest episode of our Curious Universe podcast, hear some of the first reactions from Artemis II astronauts after their Moon mission: https://go.nasa.gov/3ODuABX

user.name: NASA - National Aeronautics and Space Administration

text:
And everything under the Sun is in tune 🎶

This image from the eclipse during the Artemis II lunar flyby captures a halo of light around the Moon. Scientists are still investigating if the glow comes from interstellar dust or the solar corona.

media.ocrText: A solar eclipse, captured from a camera mounted on one of the Orion spacecraft’s solar array wings during the Artemis II crew’s flyby of the Moon’s far side. The Moon is dark, save for a bright halo of white light surrounding it. The Orion spacecraft is in the leftmost half of the image, mostly shadowed.

user.name: NASA - National Aeronautics and Space Administration

text:
Now that the Artemis II crew is home, what's next for our Artemis program?

We're preparing to launch Artemis missions every year. Artemis III is next up in 2027, with Artemis IV landing on the Moon in 2028.

Learn more about the Artemis mission cadence: https://go.nasa.gov/4dLJ1y4

media.ocrText: The crew of Artemis II (from left: Reid Wiseman, Christina Koch, Jeremy Hansen, Victor Glover) pose for a group photo after viewing the Orion spacecraft in the well deck of USS John P. Murtha in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of California. Credit: NASA/Bill Ingalls

user.name: NASA - National Aeronautics and Space Administration

text:
New photos from the Moon!

We're continuing to unveil new images from the Artemis II mission—including these two photos from April 6, showing a crescent Earthrise and a closeup of the lunar farside. Keep up with the latest: https://www.nasa.gov/artemis-ii-multimedia/

media.ocrText: A crescent Earth rises over the horizon of the Moon, which is cutting into Earth's bottom-right edge. The Moon itself is mostly in shadow. The Orion spacecraft is partially visible on the image's far left. Credit: NASA
The dimly lit far side of the Moon arcs from the bottom-left to top-right of this image. Its surface is covered in circular craters. Credit: NASA

user.name: NASA - National Aeronautics and Space Administration

text:
Our Artemis II Moon mission is complete!
 
✅ Space Launch System rocket launched crew into space
✅ Orion spacecraft provided a safe “home away from home” for astronauts
✅ Flew around the Moon, observed its far side, and conducted science
✅ New human spaceflight distance record 
✅ Crew safely returned to Earth
✅ Inspired the WORLD

text: Artemis II may have splashed down, but our photos and videos from the mission are still rolling in! Keep an eye on the latest: https://www.nasa.gov/artemis-ii-multimedia/

media.ocrText: Artemis II astronauts Reid Wiseman and Jeremy Hansen, wearing orange flight suits, sit on the edge of a helicopter, flanked by uniformed personnel. Both astronauts are grinning, and Reid is pointing at the camera. Credit: NASA/Bill Ingalls

Artemis II astronauts Victor Glover and Christina Koch, wearing orange flight suits, sit on the edge of a helicopter, flanked by uniformed personnel. Both astronauts are grinning. Credit: NASA/Bill Ingalls

user.name: NASA - National Aeronautics and Space Administration

text:
HOME.
 
The Artemis II crew has arrived back on Earth, ending a nearly 10-day journey around the Moon. The trip took them farther into space than humans have ever gone before, and now they're safely home with us.

https://go.nasa.gov/3Q47RiP

media.ocrText: Artemis II's Orion spacecraft splashes down in the Pacific Ocean against a clear blue sky. Three large striped parachutes billow above it. Credit: NASA/Joel Kowsky

user.name: NASA - National Aeronautics and Space Administration

text:
Welcome home Reid, Victor, Christina, and Jeremy! 🫶
 
The NASA Artemis II astronauts have splashed down at 8:07 p.m. EDT (0007 UTC), bringing their historic 10-day mission around the Moon to an end.

text:
Your close personal friends the Artemis II crew can't wait to get home!
 
In the meantime, enjoy a few new pictures from their camera roll. And watch their return with us live at nasa.gov/live.

media.ocrText: Earth peeks just above the horizon of the Moon, which looms large in the foreground. The Moon's surface is covered in craters of various sizes, giving it a spongy, bumpy texture. Earth's upper edge is a dreamy light blue with white clouds.
The crescent Moon, its upper two-thirds in shadow. The visible part of the Moon is a bumpy gray smile against the black of space.

user.name: NASA - National Aeronautics and Space Administration

text:
“You are special, in all of this emptiness. This is a whole bunch of nothing, this thing we call the universe. You have this oasis, this beautiful place that we get to exist together.”
 
In this video clip, Artemis II pilot Victor Glover reflects on our shared spaceship: Earth.

user.name: NASA - National Aeronautics and Space Administration

text:
Homeward bound 🌎

Artemis II astronauts have flown around the Moon, traveling 252,756 miles from Earth—farther than any other humans. They observed the lunar surface like never before, capturing iconic views. 

Now, they’re coming home. The crew will splash down in the Pacific Ocean on Friday, April 10, around 8:07 p.m. EDT (0007 UTC April 11). Help us welcome them home: www.nasa.gov/ways-to-watch/

text:
Behind the four astronauts of Artemis II are hundreds of people tracking their every move: monitoring spacecraft systems, evaluating crew safety, and staying in constant communication. The job requires sleepless nights and a level of teamwork that verges on a mind meld.

Let’s hear it for the team in Mission Control responsible for getting the astronauts around the Moon and safely home.

media.ocrText: A view inside of NASA’s Mission Control Center. There are rows of desks with multiple monitors on each. People are sitting at all of the desks. The far wall is covered by massive screens showing data and visualizations and the words “Mission Control Center” at the top. Credit: NASA

A woman sits at a desk at Mission Control. She is angled to the right with her arm outstretched as she talks to someone. On the desk in front of her are multiple screens with data and visualizations. In the background, on the far wall, are even more screens. Credit: NASA
Photograph of NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman and two other individuals looking at computer screens in Mission Control at NASA’s Johnson Space Center. Credit: NASA

user.name: NASA - National Aeronautics and Space Administration

text:
Moon flyby. Moon science. Moon capsule. Moon JOY.

The Artemis II crew has taken us along on a whirlwind tour of the Moon, testing the Orion capsule that will eventually return us to the lunar surface to stay. Reid, Victor, Christina, Jeremy, and Rise traveled farther into space than any humans before.

We knew we'd get loads of data from their mission, from crucial analysis of the spacecraft's operations to brand new observations of the lunar surface. What we didn't expect? Just how much joy the crew would bring as well. Ten days in space, endless Moon joy

text:
They're halfway home. 
 
The Artemis II astronauts have hit the "halfway" mark between the Moon and the Earth. They will splash down in the Pacific Ocean around 8:07 pm ET on Friday, April 10 (0007 UTC on Saturday, April 11), off the coast of San Diego.

media.ocrText: A sliver of Earth is illuminated against the blackness of space in this photo taken by an Artemis II crew member through an Orion spacecraft window on the third day of the mission. Credit: NASA

user.name: NASA - National Aeronautics and Space Administration

text:
Our Artemis II astronauts are headed back to Earth after their test flight around the Moon.

Listen to the latest episode of our Curious Universe podcast to learn how we'll bring the crew home: https://go.nasa.gov/47UglPz

text:
Solar eclipse in space 🚀🌘☀️

The Artemis II crew had the rare opportunity to see a solar eclipse from space as they flew around the far side of the Moon on April 6. As the Sun disappears behind the Moon, it reveals a glowing halo around the lunar disk. Science team members are investigating whether this effect is due to the corona, zodiacal light, or a combination of the two.

This video stitches together views from Orion’s solar array wing cameras to show the progression of the eclipse as seen from the capsule. The image framing moves because of small changes in Orion’s orientation throughout the eclipse.

Credit: NASA

text:
Artemis II is locked in 🔒 

During lunar flyby, the Artemis II crew spent 7 hours taking turns capturing science data and taking photos out of the Orion spacecraft window. They reported observations of the lunar surface, including nuances in color, that will help us better understand the Moon.

media.ocrText: Reid Wiseman looking out a window in the Orion spacecraft. The interior of the spacecraft is mostly dark. Wiseman’s face is brightly lit by a combination of light from outside the window and the glow of a screen in front of him. His face is upturned to look out the window above him. Credit: NASA

Christina Koch in the Orion spacecraft. She is smiling at the camera and wears glasses and a headlamp. The interior of the spacecraft is mostly dark except for the bright screen of a tablet on the right and some areas that glow blue and green. Credit: NASA

Victor Glover in the Orion spacecraft. His head is tilted back to look out a window above him, obscuring his face from the camera. The interior of the spacecraft is dark. Glover is mostly cast in shadow, except for his side profile. Credit: NASA

Jeremy Hansen takes a photograph out the window of the Orion spacecraft window. Hansen has the viewfinder of the camera pressed against his face and his left hand is adjusting the lens. Around him, the interior of the spacecraft is dark except for a brightly glowing screen in front of him and some areas of red glow. Credit: NASA

text: There's a lot to process on Day 8 of the NASA Artemis II mission. With Earth in view from Orion's windows, the astronauts are packing up and reflecting on their lunar journey.

text:
But wait, there's more!
These newly released photos show off striking details on the far side of the Moon, like craters of various sizes and basins. See new photos here: https://www.nasa.gov/gallery/lunar-flyby/

media.ocrText: The line between night and day, or the terminator, is at the top of this image of the Moon. As the Artemis II crew described, the terminator is "anything but a straight line." The Moon's surface is heavily cratered at the top, but the number of craters tapers off as you continue downward. Credit: NASA

The small, bright spot in the center of the image is the crater that the Artemis II crew have proposed as Carroll, after Commander Reid Wiseman’s late wife. About 3.5 miles across (5.6 km in diameter), the proposed Carroll crater is on the nearside of the lunar surface on the western edge and would be visible from Earth with powerful telescopes. Credit: NASA

text:
Some were born great…… and some were DESIGNED great.

I wouldn’t be here if it weren’t for the California student who designed me, Lucas Ye. He submitted his design to the Moon Mascot contest — and I was chosen to fly aboard the Artemis II mission!!!!!

I was really, really, really, REALLY surprised! And happy! -Rise

user.name: NASA - National Aeronautics and Space Administration

text:
It's Rise's time to shine! 🌟

What’s it like to be a zero gravity indicator flying around the Moon with your astronaut besties? Find out as our favorite Moon Mascot takes over the NASA Artemis account today. Follow along, and ask questions to learn about Rise's important role!

media.ocrText: A selfie-style image of Rise, Artemis II’s zero gravity indicator in front of the Space Launch System (SLS) Moon rocket. The scene is outdoors on a clear and sunny day. Credit: NASA/Christian Elliott

user.name: NASA - National Aeronautics and Space Administration

text:
Since the Gemini missions of the mid‑1960s, we’ve had a tradition of playing music to wake up astronauts and signal the start of their workday.

For the Artemis II mission, the crew personally selected their official wake‑up songs and we’ve added them to a playlist for everyone to enjoy: https://open.spotify.com/user/nasaspotify.

Stay tuned to find out which songs they’ll choose next.

media.ocrText: Four astronauts float close together inside a spacecraft. They are wearing matching black shirts, and the area around them is filled with equipment, cables, and storage bags. A large bundle wrapped in blue straps sits in the foreground. A small, round plush toy is attached to the arm of one crew member. Behind them, American and Canadian flags are attached to the wall along with other gear.

user.name: NASA - National Aeronautics and Space Administration

text:
“You can see the surface of the Moon…we just went sci-fi.”
On flight day seven, images from our NASA Artemis II crew amazed, turning science fiction to science reality. From the lunar far side to a solar eclipse from the Moon, the views are EVERYTHING.
No pressure to pick a favorite.

user.name: NASA - National Aeronautics and Space Administration

text:
Sky full of stars.

Following a successful lunar flyby, the Artemis II astronauts captured this breathtaking photo of our galaxy, the Milky Way, on April 7, 2026.

media.ocrText: A starfield filled with thousands of stars and shining clouds of dust. The Milky Way’s elegant spiral structure is dominated by just two arms wrapping off the ends of a central bar of stars. Spanning more than 100,000 light-years, Earth is located along one of the galaxy’s spiral arms, about halfway from the center. Credit: NASA

user.name: NASA - National Aeronautics and Space Administration

text:
It's not just a phase 🌕

Artemis II astronauts captured these views as the Orion spacecraft flew around the far side of the Moon on April 6, 2026. During the lunar flyby, the crew took epic, high-resolution photographs of the lunar surface, Orion, and Earth.

See the full gallery: https://www.nasa.gov/gallery/lunar-flyby/

user.name: NASA - National Aeronautics and Space Administration

text:
Do you have rocket fever? We have something for that.

Digital creators and social media storytellers are invited to register to attend the rollout of the Artemis III core stage from NASA's Michoud Assembly Facility in New Orleans later this month. Registration is open from April 7-10: https://www.nasa.gov/general/experience-the-rollout-of-sls-hardware-for-artemis-iii/

media.ocrText: NASA and Boeing prepare the butterscotch-orange-colored SLS (Space Launch System) rocket core stage for shipment at NASA’s Michoud Assembly Facility in New Orleans. The core stage is on its side on two orange structures that hold it above the ground. The core stage is just in front of a tall rectangular building with a NASA meatball logo on the side facing us. The building's massive doors are open. Credit: NASA/Eric Bordelon

user.name: NASA - National Aeronautics and Space Administration

text:
Hello, Moon. It’s great to be back.
 
Here’s a look at what the Artemis II astronauts photographed during their flight around the Moon. Check out more photos from the mission: https://www.nasa.gov/artemis-ii-multimedia/

media.ocrText: A crescent Earth setting behind the Moon’s horizon. Credit: NASA
Earth setting behind the Moon as seen by the Artemis II crew. Over half the left side of the image is filled by the gray lunar surface, pocked with craters. Credit: NASA
A close view of the Moon. Jagged circles of craters dot the gray surface, fading to dark on the left side of the image. Credit: NASA
A crescent Earth setting behind a hemisphere of the Moon. Credit: NASA
A close view of the edge of the Moon. Jagged circles of craters dot the dark gray lunar surface, which arcs across the image. Credit: NASA

user.name: NASA - National Aeronautics and Space Administration
NASA - National Aeronautics and Space Administration

text:
The Artemis II astronauts are about to make history. Watch with us as they fly around the Moon.
The crew – NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, and Christina Koch, and CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Jeremy Hansen – will come within 4,000 to 6,000 miles of the Moon's surface as they swing around the far side of the Moon. They will be the first people to see some parts of the Moon with their own eyes.
They are also on track to set a record for the farthest anyone has traveled from Earth, breaking the current record – 248,655 miles away – set in 1970 by the Apollo 13 crew.

text:
Anyone else have a case of the Moondays? 🌕

Today our Artemis II astronauts fly around the Moon! Tune in, starting at 1 p.m. EDT (1700 UTC) as they view parts of the Moon never seen by human eyes.

Watch it live with us: https://www.nasa.gov/ways-to-watch/

media.ocrText:
Graphic with Artemis II Flyby Day schedule in EDT. The lunar flyby events stream on HBO MAX, Netflix, YouTube, Peacock, Amazon Prime, and on the NASA+ app. 
 
Flyby Day Schedule (all times EDT)

ARTEMIS II CREW PASSES THE APOLLO 13 DISTANCE RECORD – 1:56 p.m. 
Crew remarks- 2:10 p.m.

PREDICTED LOSS OF COMMUNICATION AS CREW HEADS BEHIND THE MOON  (ESTIMATED TO LAST 40 MINUTES) – 6:44 p.m. 
ARTEMIS II CREW MAKES CLOSEST APPROACH TO THE MOON – 7:02 p.m. 
ARTEMIS II CREW REACHES MAXIMUM DISTANCE FROM THE EARTH  - 7:07 p.m. 
PREDICTED ACQUISITION OF SIGNAL WITH INTEGRITY – 7:25 p.m. 
ECLIPSE PERIOD BEGINS WITH MOON ECLIPSING SUN – 8:35 p.m.  
LUNAR OBSERVATION PERIOD (FLYBY) CONCLUDES – 9:20 p.m. 
SOLAR ECLIPSE PERIOD ENDS – 9:32 p.m. 
NASA+ COVERAGE CONCLUDES - 9:45 p.m.

text:
Make new friends, but keep the old.
 
This new photo from the Artemis II crew features a combined view of the Moon’s near and far sides.
 
🌓 The near side, visible on the right, is identifiable by the dark splotches that cover its surface, created early in the Moon’s history when it was volcanically active. This is the side of the Moon we can see from Earth.
 
The large crater west of the lava flows is Orientale basin, a nearly 600-mile-wide crater that straddles the Moon’s near and far sides. The Artemis II crew are the first people to ever see the full Orientale Basin.
 
🌗 Everything to the left of the crater is the far side, the hemisphere we don’t get to see from Earth because the Moon rotates on its axis at the same rate that it orbits round us.

media.ocrText: The Moon against the black of space. The right half is heavily marked with darker splotches and craters, including a very large patch that fills most of the upper right quadrant. The left side of the Moon, which is not visible from Earth, is much more uniformly gray. It has small divots and craters, but they do not change the surface color. There is one prominent darker spot between 7 and 8 o'clock on the Moon's surface.

text:
Wake up ✅ 
Shave ✅ 
See something no human has ever seen before 
 
The Artemis II crew is getting ready to make history. Later today, they’ll fly around the far side of the Moon, seeing parts of the lunar surface never seen before. Coverage of the lunar flyby begins at 1 p.m. EDT (1700 UTC).

media.ocrText: Jeremy Hansen shaves his face, using an electric shaver, inside the Orion capsule. In his right hand, he is holding his smartphone like he's taking a selfie, to use as a mirror. He is surrounded by cords and bags attached to the walls. The capsule walls are padded. He is locked in, focusing on the job of shaving. Credit: NASA

Two crew sleeping bags are tied down with cord inside the Orion capsule. They are stretched across the image, on either side of various components and instruments. The scene is dimly illuminated so it glows with a greenish light. The sleeping bags are quilted, with rivets around the edges. Credit: NASA
